title: Josh and Chuck's Warm and Cozy Christmas Extravaganza 2013
summary: Holiday special episode of Stuff You Should Know covering Christmas topics. The hosts tell the origin story of Rudolph the Red Nose Reindeer, correcting a popular myth: Robert May, a copywriter at Montgomery Ward in Chicago, wrote the 1939 story for a coloring book, and after he was pressed to give up the copyright, the company's head Sewell Avery signed it back to him. Johnny Marks, May's brother-in-law, wrote the famous song, and the 1964/1965 stop-motion special is discussed. Next, a story about Mia and her dog Marley, a King Charles Spaniel stolen from outside a New York store on Christmas Eve 2012 and recovered by a woman who bought him in Union Square and took him to a vet who found his microchip. Then modern Santa Claus careers: the costs of Santa suits, boots, gloves and beards, the Kringle Group poll on Santas' germs and wardrobes, the Charles W. Howard Santa Claus School in Midland, Michigan, and Santa pay. Then hot buttered rum: its colonial history with Medford rum, the difference between a toddy and a sling, ingredients, the traditional hot-poker method, a simpler modern recipe, and a batter variation. The episode closes with a reading of O. Henry's The Gift of the Magi.

segments.summary: The hosts welcome listeners to the 2013 Christmas Extravaganza, tease the hot buttered rum segment, and set up the holiday episode.

segments.title: Origin of Rudolph the Red Nose Reindeer
segments.summary: The story of how Robert May, a Montgomery Ward copywriter, created Rudolph in 1939 for a coloring book, named him, and had the story and character developed; Montgomery Ward's head Sewell Avery later signed the copyright back to May.

segments.title: Rudolph's creation, copyright and differences from the song and cartoon
segments.summary: Rudolph's coloring book became a hit, but May did not own the rights. He asked Montgomery Ward to return the copyright and was granted it. Brother-in-law Johnny Marks wrote the song and the 1964 stop-motion special was narrated by Burl Ives. The original Rudolph was not one of Santa's reindeer and his parents were not embarrassed by him; Santa found him by accident on a foggy night.

segments.title: Robert May's later life
segments.summary: The hosts note May lived a successful life afterward and returned to work at Montgomery Ward even though he no longer needed to work.

segments.title: Christmas 2012 stolen dog Marley returned
segments.summary: Seven-year-old Mia and her mother lost their Cavalier King Charles Spaniel Marley when it was stolen outside a New York store on Christmas Eve 2012. A woman later saw a man selling the shivering dog in Union Square, bought it for $220, and took it to a vet, which found the microchip; the family was reunited on Christmas Day and the thief was arrested.

segments.title: Famous mall Santas
segments.summary: The hosts recall a highly realistic mall Santa from North Towne mall in the 1970s and discuss how well-regarded Santa actors can be.

segments.title: Costs of becoming a Santa
segments.summary: A good Santa suit costs about two thousand dollars, boots about eight hundred, white leather gloves about three hundred, and a yak-hair beard around a thousand to twelve thousand dollars; a white beard dye job costs about six hundred. Santas often need backup suits.

segments.title: Kringle Group poll on Santa life and Santa school
segments.summary: A Kringle Group poll says twenty percent of mall Santas have five or six suits and most have at least two. Seventy-five percent get sneezed on, and many are coughed on or sneezed on up to fifteen times a day. The Charles W. Howard Santa Claus School in Midland, Michigan, teaches Santas about Christmas history and reindeer, as the reindeer should all be females with antlers.

segments.title: Santa pay and career earnings
segments.summary: Santas can earn roughly eight to twelve thousand dollars, sometimes up to around fifty thousand, over a few months of the season, with the best city mall Santas earning the most.

segments.title: History of hot buttered rum and toddies
segments.summary: Hot buttered rum is a type of hot toddy, which is a hot drink of liquor, water and sugar; a sling is the cold version. Rum was a major colonial product, with Medford rum an important part of the New England economy. Hot buttered rum was popular in New England by the mid-eighteenth century, and George Washington reportedly loved it.

segments.title: Hot buttered rum ingredients and butter debate
segments.summary: The hosts discuss using unsalted, good-quality butter and dark rum. Cocktail historian David Wondrich is quoted as a purist who opposes batter versions; a Gun Club Drink Book author said the butter only lubricates the mustache, while the article's author called butter a key part of the drink.

segments.title: How to make hot buttered rum
segments.summary: The traditional method heats a mug, adds rum, sugar, water and about two tablespoons of butter, then plunges a hot poker into the mix. A modern method uses boiling water and stirring instead, with nutmeg grated on top. A batter version uses butter, cinnamon, nutmeg, clove and brown sugar, scooped into each drink.

segments.title: Reading: The Gift of the Magi by O. Henry (part 1)
segments.summary: The hosts begin a reading of O. Henry's The Gift of the Magi, in which Della sells her hair for twenty dollars to buy a platinum fob chain for Jim, who has sold his watch.

segments.title: Reading: The Gift of the Magi (part 2)
segments.summary: Della's sacrifice of her hair is revealed to Jim, who reveals he has sold his watch to buy her tortoiseshell combs; the story closes with its moral about gift-givers being the wisest.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts exchange Merry Christmas wishes and close the episode.
